She put down the dish towel and went out onto the porch. The air smelled wrong—not the usual brine and rot of kelp, but something colder, mineral, like the inside of a cave. Gulls were absent. That was the part that stayed with her later: no gulls at all, not even the one-legged one that begged at the fish shed every evening.

Down the shore, Tobias Reel was dragging his skiff up past the dune grass, moving faster than she had seen him move in twenty years. He did not wave. He did not look at the water either, which was strange, because everyone in Hollow Point looked at the water. It was the one thing they all did.

Maren went back inside and took the lantern from its hook. Then she stood for a long moment in the doorway, thinking of her mother, who had always said the sea kept its own time and lent none of it to anyone.

She went down the porch steps and along the path toward the fish shed, keeping the dune between herself and the water. Tobias had gotten his skiff up as far as the shed wall and was lashing it to the iron ring there with hands that would not stop shaking. He was a man who could splice a line in a gale. "Tobias."

He flinched. Then he saw it was her and some of the stiffness went out of his shoulders, though not much.

"Go up to the church," he said. "Take the road, not the beach."

"What is it?"

He finished the knot, wrong, and left it. "My grandfather's time, it came in like this once. Early. Quiet." He wiped his mouth. "The ones who looked didn't come up the hill after."

"Looked at what?"

But he was already walking, head bowed as if into rain, and he passed her without another word. It had a little light in it, low, the colour of a lamp through curtain. She knew that light. She had lit it herself every winter evening of her life, in the front room, and she had not lit it tonight.

She turned her head, slowly, the way you turn to a sound behind you. The house stood on its rise with every window dark.

She turned back. The light was still there in the water, and now there was something in front of it. Not a shape. A thinness in the glow, the way a person standing in a doorway makes less of the room behind them.

Maren got up onto her knees in the sand that would not drift. The dark was at her wrists.

The thinness in the glow did a small thing. It leaned, the way a person leans to see past a curtain, and the lamp behind it brightened by the width of a shoulder. Then it was still again. It had looked out. That was all. It had come to the window of the front room and looked out at the sea, and the sea was where Maren was.

She found she had put her hand to her own collar, the way you do when you have been seen in your coat and not your dress.

Post nine knocked. Nearer than the others. The sound had a room around it now.

The dark was at her elbows. It did not pull. It did not even seem to want her; it only came up, the way the level in a jug comes up, and whatever was in it was in it.

She thought of the road. Tobias on it, not looking back, his boots going up the hill in the dark towards the church. She tried to picture the hill behind her and found that she could not. Not the road, not the church, not the fish shed with its ring. There was the house, every window dark, and there was the slope she knelt on, and the slope went down. That was the only direction it had.

In the water the figure raised its hand, once, flat, the way you wave to someone a long way out. Then it stepped aside from the lamp, and the doorway was just a doorway, and the room behind it was lit and empty and waiting to be come into.
